messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sara, a 63-year-old Middle Eastern woman who works as an auditor, has been struggling with the traumatic aftermath of losing her sister in a hiking accident. The vivid and haunting memories of that day have left Sara feeling perpetually on guard and deeply mistrustful of life's uncertainties. The trauma began when Sara’s sister died in a remote mountainous area where they were hiking together. Being confined to a small, isolated space during the search efforts after the incident has left Sara with an intense aversion to being in locked or confined rooms. The sight of any natural environment reminiscent of that fateful hike is enough to trigger her memories and send her into a state of heightened anxiety. When Sara finds herself in nature, she cannot help but be transported back to the moment when her sister fell. Every sound and sight feels magnified and real, and this sensory reliving brings back the same terror she felt at that time. The suddenness with which these memories come, triggered by something as simple as a rustling leaf or the scent of pine, leaves Sara feeling overwhelmed. This hypervigilance has extended to her daily life. She avoids going to unfamiliar places because she feels unable to assess the danger accurately. This constant state of alertness makes it difficult for her to fall asleep or stay asleep at night, leading to chronic fatigue and irritability. Her fear of not being able to predict or control potentially dangerous situations is a direct result of these intrusive memories. Sara’s experience has also led her to lose faith in both people and the idea of a higher power that could prevent such tragedies from occurring. The body’s instinctive reactions, which keep Sara feeling as though she is still in danger even when she is safe at home or work, have only reinforced this sense of helplessness. This belief that bad things will inevitably happen has made it nearly impossible for her to trust anyone or anything. Her negative appraisals are deeply intertwined with the triggers and threats she faces daily. The more Sara feels helpless and distrustful, the greater her fear becomes. Her hypervigilance is exacerbated by these thoughts, making each trigger all the more potent in bringing back the full memory of that day. This cycle has left Sara feeling increasingly isolated and anxious about her safety. As an auditor, Sara’s work environment often requires travel to unfamiliar locations for audits. However, her fear of going to new places has made it difficult for her to fulfill these duties effectively. Her boss has noticed a decline in her performance due to frequent absences and an inability to focus during critical meetings. This occupational impact is just one of the many ways that Sara’s symptoms have affected her life. Recently, Sara's mounting anxiety and sleeplessness reached a breaking point when she experienced a panic attack at work, prompting her to seek help. She fears being trapped in this state of constant fear and hopes for a way out of the debilitating cycle she has found herself in. Despite her initial reluctance, Sara recognizes that without intervention, these symptoms will continue to erode her sense of safety and trust in the world around her.
